chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Angel Investing Really Is

lessons.title: Angels vs Venture Capital vs Private Equity: Who Funds What Stage

children.text: In 2010, Zomato was a restaurant-menu website run out of Delhi, and its first outside cheque was ₹4.7 crore. Eleven years later it raised ₹9,375 crore in an IPO. Between those two points, the company took money from a listed internet company, venture capital funds, a Singapore state investor and Alibaba's payments affiliate. Each arrived at a different moment, wrote a different size of cheque and wanted a different kind of return. By the end of this lesson you will know who funds which stage, how angels, VCs and PE firms each make money, and why their interests do not always line up with yours.

body.text: Angels, venture capital and private equity are not rivals chasing the same deal. They are runners in a relay: each takes the baton at a different stage, with different money, different risk and a different definition of success.

children.text: Three Kinds of Investors, Three Kinds of Money

markDefs.definition: The investors who put money into a fund, such as pension funds, insurers, family offices and HNIs. They commit capital but do not make the fund's investment decisions.
The firm that raises and manages a fund, picks the investments and earns fees plus a share of profits.

children.text: The cleanest way to tell these investors apart is to ask one question: whose money is it? An angel invests personal savings. A venture capital (VC) or private equity (PE) firm invests a fund pooled from
limited partners
, and the firm itself acts as the
general partner

. In India, most domestic VC funds are registered with SEBI as Category I AIFs, and most PE funds as Category II AIFs. That one difference, own money versus other people's money, shapes everything else: how much they invest, how fast they decide and what they need from a winner.

body.title: How a VC or PE fund earns money for itself

children.text: Fund managers are paid in two ways, often summarised as "2 and 20", although the exact numbers vary from fund to fund:
Management fee:
around 2% of the fund a year, which pays salaries and running costs whether or not investments do well.
Carried interest:
around 20% of the profits, usually paid only after limited partners get their money back plus a minimum hurdle return.
An angel pays no one. There is no fee and no carry, but there is also no professional team doing the research, negotiating the terms or chasing the founder for updates. That work is yours.
The Funding Relay: Following Zomato

events.title: Foodiebay is born
events.description: Deepinder Goyal and Pankaj Chaddah start a website listing restaurant menus in Delhi. The founders' own time and money are the only capital.

events.title: First outside cheque
events.description: Info Edge, the listed parent of Naukri.com, invests ₹4.7 crore. It plays the role an angel usually plays: backing a young company before it is proven.

events.title: Venture capital arrives
events.description: Sequoia Capital, whose India arm is now called Peak XV Partners, invests as Zomato expands across cities and countries.

events.title: Large growth rounds
events.description: Zomato raises $60 million in a round led by Temasek, the Singapore state-owned investor.

events.title: Strategic late-stage money
events.description: Ant Financial, Alibaba's payments affiliate, invests $210 million as food delivery becomes the core business.

events.title: IPO on NSE and BSE
events.description: Zomato raises ₹9,375 crore from public investors, and early backers can finally sell shares in the market.

body.text: Notice the pattern. With each step, the business became less risky, the cheques became bigger and the investors became more institutional. The earliest backer took the most risk for the smallest cheque, and earned the largest multiple. That is the seat an angel sits in.

children.text: Where the Money Actually Goes in India
Seed rounds get the headlines on startup Twitter, but they are a small share of the money. Most capital flows to companies that have already proven something.

body.title: Read the donut
body.prompt: Late-stage rounds raised $5.5 billion of the $10.5 billion total in 2025. What percentage of all funding was late stage? Round to the nearest whole number.
body.explanation: 5.5 ÷ 10.5 = 0.524, or about 52%. More than half of all startup capital went to companies that already had scale, which is also why rounds fell about 39% while total money fell only 17%: investors wrote fewer, larger cheques into proven businesses.

children.text: Why a VC Wants a Different Outcome Than You

markDefs.definition: A single investment large enough to pay back the entire fund on its own.

children.text: A VC fund backs perhaps a few dozen companies and knows most will disappoint. So every investment is judged by one question: can this company, on its own, return the whole fund? Investors call such a company a
fund returner
. The maths is simple:

body.latex: \text{Exit value needed to return the fund} = \frac{\text{Fund size}}{\text{Ownership at exit}} = \frac{500\text{ crore}}{10\%} = 5{,}000\text{ crore}
body.caption: A ₹500 crore fund that owns 10% of a company at exit needs that company to sell or list at ₹5,000 crore just to return the fund once.

children.text: Now go back to KhetSetu from the last lesson. Say an agritech company offers ₹300 crore to buy it in year 6. You invested ₹10 lakh at a ₹10 crore post-money valuation and have been diluted from 1% to 0.5%. Your stake is worth ₹1.5 crore, a 15x return. The VC fund that owns 10% gets ₹30 crore, which is just 6% of its ₹500 crore fund. For you, it is a life-changing exit. For the VC, it barely moves the needle, and it may push the founder to reject the offer and swing for something much bigger.

body.caption: The same ₹300 crore acquisition, seen from two seats (illustrative)

cells: 6% of the fund, not enough to matter

body.title: Find the fund returner
body.prompt: A ₹300 crore seed fund expects to own 8% of its best company at exit. What exit valuation, in ₹ crore, does that company need to return the whole fund once?
body.explanation: ₹300 crore ÷ 8% = ₹300 crore ÷ 0.08 = ₹3,750 crore. Anything smaller and the fund needs several winners to break even, before it even thinks about a profit.

body.text: Do not copy VC maths with your own money. A VC fund can absorb many failures because it holds a few dozen companies, has a decade to wait and is paid a management fee along the way. An angel with three cheques and no fee income has none of those cushions.

children.text: Private Equity: The Opposite End of the Relay

PE investors rarely touch startups. In 2016, Blackstone agreed to buy Hewlett Packard Enterprise's 60.5% stake in Mphasis at ₹430 per share, in a deal worth up to ₹7,071 crore including the mandatory open offer to public shareholders. Mphasis was a listed, profitable Bengaluru IT services company with decades of client relationships. Blackstone was not betting that the business would survive. It was betting it could run an established business better and sell it for more.

body.label: Where the angel sits in the relay
body.value: First money in: highest risk, smallest cheque, biggest potential multiple
body.context: Every later investor pays a higher price for a less risky company. The angel's edge is getting in early; the cost is facing the highest chance of total loss.

body.title: Who is the natural investor?
body.question: A 30-year-old, profitable pump manufacturer in Coimbatore with ₹400 crore in annual revenue wants to sell a 51% stake so the founding family can partly cash out. Which investor type is the most natural fit?
body.explanation: A mature, profitable business selling a controlling stake is classic private equity territory. Angels and seed VCs look for young companies with huge growth potential, and none of them would buy control of a ₹400 crore manufacturer.

body.title: Sort the pitches
body.scenario:
Rakesh, a Lucknow business owner with surplus capital, is introduced to three companies in one week.
A: Two IIT Kanpur graduates with a working prototype of an EV battery-swapping station, raising ₹1.5 crore.
B: A Chennai software company with ₹40 crore in annual recurring revenue, growing 60% a year, raising ₹150 crore.
C: A family-owned dairy business in Gujarat with ₹600 crore in revenue and steady profits, whose promoters want to sell part of their stake.
body.prompt: Which type of investor naturally funds each company? Which one, if any, could Rakesh realistically back as an angel?
body.modelAnswer:
A is angel and seed territory. The company has a prototype but no proven business, and a ₹1.5 crore round is exactly where individual angels and small seed funds write cheques. This is the only realistic option for Rakesh as an angel.
B is venture capital territory. With ₹40 crore of recurring revenue and 60% growth, it is raising a growth round far too large for individual angels; VC funds lead rounds like this.
C is private equity territory. It is mature, profitable and looking for a partial exit for promoters, which is what PE funds buy.
The lesson: the stage of the company decides the investor, not the other way round. An angel who tries to squeeze into a ₹150 crore round usually gets a tiny allocation on worse terms than the funds leading it.

body.title: Name the fund investors
body.textWithBlank: Pension funds, insurers and family offices that put money into a VC or PE fund are called limited ___.
body.explanation: Limited partners (LPs) provide the capital. The fund manager, the general partner (GP), decides where it is invested and earns fees and carried interest.

cards.definition: A pooled fund that buys minority stakes in young, fast-growing companies and relies on a few big winners.
A pooled fund that invests in mature, usually profitable businesses, often buying control.
An investor, such as a pension fund or family office, who commits money to a VC or PE fund.
The firm that manages a fund, picks investments and earns fees plus carried interest.
The fund manager's share of profits, commonly around 20%, usually paid after investors get their capital back plus a hurdle return.
A single investment large enough to pay back the entire fund on its own.

points: Angels invest their own money; VC and PE firms invest pooled funds from limited partners and charge fees plus carried interest.
Angels fund ideas and prototypes, VCs fund proven traction and rapid growth, and PE funds buy into mature, usually profitable businesses.
As a company grows, risk falls, cheques rise and investors become more institutional, as Zomato's journey from a ₹4.7 crore first cheque to a ₹9,375 crore IPO shows.
More than half of Indian startup funding in 2025 went to late-stage companies; seed rounds were only about 10%.
A VC needs fund-returning outcomes, so an exit that is excellent for an angel can be too small for the VC on the same cap table.
Do not copy VC portfolio maths with your own money: you lack their diversification, time horizon and fee income.
